entries.context: Game title, largest text on the title screen. Product name; keep untranslated unless marketing provides a localized name.
Subtitle under the game title: the name of the first mystery case. 'Lantern Lane' is the street's name.
Title screen button that starts the case from the beginning. Short, fits a child-sized button.
Title screen button that resumes saved progress. Shown only when a save exists.
Development-build-only button on a small paper pill with a globe icon, bottom-right of the title screen. {0} is the native name of the current language, e.g. 'English'.
Small corner label for testers. {0} is the app version, {1} is a build identifier. Not translated by marketing.

Small second line on the title screen's Continue button, under 'Continue'. {0} is the case question the player has open, e.g. 'How did June get in?' (never a step of the route); {1} is how many paper bats the player has found, e.g. 7. Keep it under about 28 characters.

First prompt after starting, shown on touch screens on a small paper tag just above the on-screen stick ghost, so 'here' means that spot. Plain instruction for children 8–12; keep it under about 24 characters.

entries.value: Use W A S D or the arrow keys to walk.
entries.context: First prompt after starting, keyboard players. Key names may stay in Latin letters.

entries.value: Use the left stick to walk.
entries.context: First prompt after starting, gamepad players.
On-screen pause button label and accessibility name. Very short.
On-screen jump button label. Very short, fits a round thumb button.
On-screen contextual action button fallback label when no specific verb applies. Shown on a small paper tag under the round orange action button; very short.

Verb on the small paper tag under the round orange action button when nothing can be examined or used nearby: pressing it makes Pip (a child in a bat costume) do a quick forward tumble while running, or a short forward dive in the air. Imperative verb, one short word; fits about 8 characters.

Verb on the small paper tag under the round orange action button while Pip (a child in a bat costume) is in the air: pressing it makes Pip do a short forward dive that lands in a tumble. Replaces 'Roll' on the same tag while airborne. Imperative verb, one short word; fits about 8 characters.

entries.value: Keep holding Jump to go much higher
entries.context: One-time tip on a small paper tag just above the round Jump button, shown the first time the player taps Jump briefly. It teaches the high jump: keeping a finger on the Jump button after take-off (not tapping it) makes Pip shoot up about twice as high. Say clearly that the button stays pressed. 'Jump' is the name of that button: keep it the same word as the button label 'ui.hud.jump'. Plain instruction for children 8-12; keep it under about 36 characters.

One-time tip on a small paper tag just above the round Jump button, shown the first time Pip lands while running: pressing Jump right at the moment of landing makes the next jump higher (up to three in a row). Encouraging tone for children 8-12; keep it under about 30 characters.

entries.value: Hold Jump while falling to glide
entries.context: One-time tip on a small paper tag just above the round Jump button, shown the first time Pip falls after a jump without gliding: keeping the Jump button pressed while coming down spreads Pip's bat cape so Pip floats down slowly. 'Jump' is that button's name, as in 'ui.hud.jump'. Keep it under about 36 characters.

entries.value: Use in the air to dive
entries.context: One-time tip on a small paper tag just above the round orange action button, shown the first time Pip is in the air after having rolled once. 'Use' means pressing that orange button (its tag reads 'Roll' on the ground and 'Dive' in the air); pressing it mid-jump makes Pip dive forward. Keep it under about 30 characters.
Heading of the pause menu.
Pause menu button that returns to play.
Pause menu button that returns to the title screen.

Settings toggle row (off by default). When on, a see-through helping hand may show how to do the next step if the player has been stuck for a few minutes; when off, it appears only when the player presses the radio hint button. One short word.
Accessibility name of a small eye icon on a clue sticker in the notebook. Tapping it replays, in the real street, what a neighbour remembers seeing (a short see-through re-enactment). Short.
Accessibility name of the round skip button (top right) during a short re-enactment of a neighbour's memory. Skipping returns to play at once. Short.

entries.value: Grown-ups: hold both spots for 3 seconds
entries.context: Small line and accessibility label on the parent gate, a screen with two marked felt spots that an adult presses and holds at the same time for 3 seconds before a download or a link that leaves the game. Addressed to the adult. Keep the number 3 as a digit.

entries.value: Grown-ups: hold both shoulder buttons for 3 seconds
entries.context: Gamepad version of the parent gate line: the same screen, but an adult with a game controller holds the two shoulder buttons (the bumpers on top of the controller, left and right) together for 3 seconds. Pictures of both bumpers sit on the two felt spots. Addressed to the adult. Use the platform-neutral word for the shoulder buttons; keep the number 3 as a digit.

entries.value: Grown-ups: hold Q and P together for 3 seconds
entries.context: Keyboard version of the parent gate line: an adult holds the Q key and the P key (far apart on the keyboard) at the same time for 3 seconds. Key caps showing Q and P sit on the two felt spots. Addressed to the adult. Keep the letters Q and P as they are; keep the number 3 as a digit.

Environmental caption for players with sound off (square brackets mark a non-speech sound). Describe only what is seen or heard. Shown once at the start, when three uneven knocks sound from the dark blue house up the street. Shown in the caption strip at the bottom of the screen, which wraps to two lines at most: keep it within about 50 characters including the brackets. A direction such as '(to the left)' is added after it, so keep it short.

Environmental caption for players with sound off (square brackets mark a non-speech sound). Describe only what is seen or heard, never what it means. Inside the hall of the blue house; three uneven knocks sound and the floorboards shake a little. Keep it within about 50 characters including the brackets. A direction such as '(to the left)' is added after it.

entries.value: Something silver flashed up high, by the side of the house!
entries.context: Bea, a fast-talking girl dressed as a pumpkin, standing by her bicycle at the plaza. Spoken line, shown as a subtitle in a speech bubble. Audience: children 6-9; keep it short and plain. First time Pip talks to her. She only saw a quick silver flash high above the hedge, by the side of the blue house; she did not see who or what it was. Never name June or a cape.

entries.value: Up high, over the hedge. Then it was gone!
entries.context: Bea, a fast-talking girl dressed as a pumpkin, standing by her bicycle at the plaza. Spoken line, shown as a subtitle in a speech bubble. Audience: children 6-9; keep it short and plain. Repeat conversation: she repeats where the silver flash was, high above the hedge, and that it vanished. Never name June or a cape.

entries.value: The door's open now? That silver flash was long before.

entries.value: Three knocks, three bows! I'm putting an owl on my bike.

entries.value: That front door? I could see it from my bench. It stayed shut.
entries.context: Mr. Vale, a friendly older neighbour dressed as a mummy, sitting on his bench by a candy cauldron. Spoken line, shown as a subtitle in a speech bubble. Audience: children 8-12; keep it short and plain. First conversation while the front door is still shut.

entries.value: Sit down and see for yourself.

entries.value: Pip! You found my secret way in! Did you hear the knocks too?

Accessibility name of the round notebook button at the top-right of the play screen, next to Pause. It opens Pip's paper case notebook. Very short.
Small hint at the bottom-right of a speech card, next to a round orange arrow button, telling the player to tap to show the next line. Short.

Gamepad and keyboard version of 'Tap to continue': small hint at the bottom-right of a speech card, next to a round orange disc that shows the button or key to press (a picture, not a word). Telling the player to press that button to show the next line. Short.
Button at the top-right during a conversation that skips the rest of it. One short word.
Name tab on the speech card when Pip, the player (a child in a bat costume), describes what they see. Character name.
Name tab on the speech card when Bea, a girl dressed as a pumpkin, is speaking. Character name.
Name tab on the speech card when Mr. Vale, an older neighbour dressed as a mummy, is speaking. Character name with a polite title.
Name tab on the speech card when June, Bea's older sister dressed as a star witch, is speaking. Character name.
Name tab on the speech card when Aunt Kit, the owner of the blue house dressed as a fortune teller, is speaking. Character name with a family title.

Caption for a sound, with where it comes from. {0} is the bracketed sound caption, e.g. '[Three knocks from the blue house]'; {1} is a direction word such as 'ahead' or 'to the left'. Shown in the caption strip next to an arrow.
Direction word inside a sound caption: the sound comes from in front of the camera. Lower case, fits inside parentheses.
Direction word inside a sound caption: the sound comes from the left of the screen. Lower case, fits inside parentheses.
Direction word inside a sound caption: the sound comes from the right of the screen. Lower case, fits inside parentheses.
Direction word inside a sound caption: the sound comes from behind the camera. Lower case, fits inside parentheses.
Accessibility name of the round X button that closes the notebook. Short.
Rubber-stamp text on a notebook question once the child has placed the right clue stickers. Very short and cheerful.

Pip is a child in a bat costume; Pip states only what is seen, heard or felt, never what it means (no deductions). Opening a small child-height wooden panel in the workshop, painted with an owl whose wings are folded.

Aunt Kit, the owner of the blue house, dressed as a fortune teller. Spoken line, shown as a subtitle in a speech bubble. Audience: children 6-9. After her owl show starts, she asks Pip to explain the case; the notebook opens on the questions the child has not answered yet. Warm, curious, never testing.

Paper notebook: a clue sticker's note, shown when the child taps the sticker. It states only what was seen, heard or said (a perception), never what it means or which question it answers. Pip tried the front door from the porch.

Accessibility name of an empty dashed slot on a notebook question, where the child places a clue sticker.
Accessibility name of a dashed question-mark outline in the clue tray: one clue the child has not found yet. Never says which.
Accessibility name (and pencil note) for a clue sticker set aside after many tries on one question. Gentle, never 'wrong'.
Accessibility name of the small place badge that lights over a clue outline when Pip is stuck; it shows the place in the street, never the answer.
Accessibility name of Pip's thought cloud on a notebook page after a set of clues that does not answer the question yet. Gentle, never 'wrong'.
Large mark drawn inside a pencil circle for a notebook question or note that is not found yet. Usually a question mark; replace with the language's own question mark if it differs.
Separator between short clue labels in the list of discoveries on the final notebook card, e.g. 'Three knocks · Bea: the cape'. Keep the spaces around it.

entries.value: Update Spooky Street to keep playing this case. Your save is kept safe.
